questions.q: In the status-driven content pipeline, which two stages always need a human, at minimum?
options: Approving the brief and editing the draft
Writing the brief and repurposing for social
Running the self-check and scheduling posts
Adding the idea and writing the first draft
questions.explain: A human touches the work at least twice: approving the brief and editing the draft. AI-written content should never publish without a human edit.

questions.q: Your drafting step keeps producing posts with convincing statistics that nobody can trace to a source. What change does the lesson recommend?
options: Ask the model to name a well-known source for every number
Forbid invented facts and have it leave a source-needed marker
Raise the effort setting so the model double-checks its numbers
Strip every number out of posts before they reach the editor
questions.explain: The drafting prompt forbids invented statistics, quotes and studies and asks for a [SOURCE NEEDED] marker wherever a fact would help. The editor then finds a real source or deletes the claim.

questions.q: The self-check step flags three unsupported claims in a draft that otherwise covers every key point. What happens next in the pipeline?
options: The draft is blocked and sent back to the drafting step
The self-check step rewrites the claims in safer wording
The editor uses the flagged claims as a fact-checking list
The claims are deleted automatically before publishing
questions.explain: Flagged claims don't block the draft. They become the editor's fact-checking list, so no claim slips through unchecked.
